Prof. Hilmi Volkan Demir is a highly respected and knowledgeable academic, and this was clearly reflected in his teaching throughout the course. His lectures were well-structured, clear, and rich in content. Despite teaching this course for the first time, he made an evident effort to ensure that students could follow each concept, and he approached the material with patience and precision. His ability to communicate complex topics in a digestible way, along with his fluent and professional English, significantly enhanced the learning experience. I particularly appreciated the depth of theoretical knowledge shared in class and his engagement with students during lectures.

The only area I personally felt could be improved was the cleanroom (fab) sessions. While the lecture part of the course was very strong, students were largely left on their own during the hands-on fab sessions. More direct support or structured guidance during these parts, either from the instructor himself or designated staff, would have helped us feel more confident in navigating the practical aspects of nanofabrication, especially for those without prior cleanroom experience.

This was a highly valuable and intellectually enriching course. I greatly appreciated Prof. Demir’s dedication to teaching, the clarity of his explanations, and the depth of expertise he brought into the classroom. I would definitely recommend this course to future students interested in micro- and nanofabrication.
He was a very good lecturer. Very understanding and chill throughout the semester.
course: The strongest aspect of the course was the well-structured and informative theoretical lectures. The content was rich, and the instructor explained complex fabrication concepts in a clear and logical manner. This theoretical foundation greatly helped us understand the field of micro- and nanofabrication, even without having extensive prior experience. The weakest part of the course, in my opinion, was the fab sessions. As someone with no prior cleanroom experience, I found these sessions extremely challenging and overwhelming. The structure was quite intense, and it was difficult to follow or grasp the procedures without step-by-step guidance. The teaching assistants were not able to provide sufficient support during this part of the course. Fortunately, the cleanroom engineers were highly helpful and experienced , without their assistance, I don’t think we would have been able to complete our final project. For future editions of the course, offering more structured supervision and clearer instructions during fab sessions would make a significant difference, especially for students encountering these techniques for the first time.

The final project is not fair for all groups, and the competition for the project is totally unfair. That is, some assistants who have more than 10 years of experience heavily help their groups. Those assistants single-handedly fabricate their team's final project while the team members of those groups are only taking notes. On the other hand, some groups ' TA is not even answering any questions or giving any feedback on the suggested flow process submitted by the group. This diversity of the TA mindset makes the competition totally unfair! In addition, I personally ran into a group whose TA was absent. Thus, I really suggest that if a competition is held next time, all TAs must have the same mentality towards helping their group members.

There was a teaching assistant assigned to the course, who also served as the lead TA responsible for overseeing the cleanroom sessions and the final project process. Although the TA seemed to have a good command of English, their accent often made communication difficult, particularly in the lab setting, where clarity is essential. Despite claiming several years of experience and acting in a lead capacity, the TA did not provide the level of support one would typically expect in such a role.

As a student with no prior cleanroom experience, I found the hands-on sessions extremely challenging. While the TA was technically present and physically accessible, their attitude was not supportive at all. They often came across as distant and unapproachable, and at times even displayed a sense of superiority that made it uncomfortable to ask for help. I did not find them to be understanding, helpful, or encouraging throughout the process. Even completing the cleanroom quizzes would not have been possible without the assistance of the cleanroom engineers, whose support was essential. I also observed that other TAs were much more involved with their assigned student groups during the final project phase, offering significantly more hands-on help. This resulted in an uneven and, in my opinion, unfair learning experience. In such a technical and demanding course, it is crucial to ensure that all student groups receive equal support.

Overall, I do not believe the lead TA contributed meaningfully to the practical aspects of the course or showed awareness of the students’ learning challenges and needs.
